Kano drug war: PCN denies shielding illicit drug dealers
items.description: …says 1,631 drug outlets sealed in 2026, challenges task force chairman to provide evidence of alleged staff involvement By Joseph Erunke, Abuja The Pharmacy Council of Nigeria (PCN) has denied allegations that it is shielding illicit drug dealers and facilitating the distribution of controlled substances in Kano State, insisting that it remains committed to enforcing pharmaceutical regulations. The council described the allegations by the Chairman of the Kano State Multi-Agency Taskforce on Drug Abuse and Illicit Trafficking, Muhuyi Magaji Rimin-Gado, as baseless and misleading, challenging him to provide verifiable evidence to substantiate his claims. In a rebuttal issued on Saturday and signed by Pharm. Hasiya Ladan, Consultant Pharmacist at the PCN Kano State Office, on behalf of the Registrar and Chief Executive Officer, the council disclosed that it sealed 1,631 pharmaceutical premises in Kano State in 2026 following inspections of 2,304 drug outlets. It also said 15 investigations into suspected regulatory violations were ongoing in the state, while its national enforcement team had visited Kano twice this year, in April and September. The rebuttal followed allegations made by Rimin-Gado at a press conference in Kano on November 14, where he accused the PCN and the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) of allegedly protecting drug dealers operating in the state. The task force chairman had, among other things, questioned the circumstances surrounding the issuance of import licences to pharmaceutical companies dealing in pregabalin, particularly after NAFDAC rescheduled the drug as a controlled substance on September 14, 2026. He also accused the PCN of registering a pharmaceutical outlet at No. 10 Apple Avenue, allegedly located in a residential area, which he claimed was being used as a concealed distribution point for the drug. Rimin-Gado further alleged that some PCN officials were involved in clandestine drug businesses and questioned the council’s capacity to effectively regulate pharmaceutical activities in Kano, citing its relatively small number of personnel in the state. However, the PCN maintained that the regulation of pharmaceutical premises was a statutory federal responsibility backed by the Constitution, legislation and judicial pronouncements. It cited Item 21 of Part I of the Second Schedule to the 1999 Constitution, arguing that drugs and poisons fall under the Exclusive Legislative List and that their regulation is therefore the responsibility of the Federal Government through authorised agencies. The council also referenced the Pharmacy Council of Nigeria (Establishment) Act 2022, the Supreme Court judgment in Pharmacists Board of Nigeria v. Franklin Adegbesote (1986), and a February 16, 2024 judgment of the Federal High Court, Kano, as legal authorities affirming its regulatory mandate. On the allegation that it registered a pharmaceutical outlet in a residential neighbourhood in violation of the Land Use Act, the council said the task force chairman had failed to identify the specific provisions of the law allegedly breached. It explained that its Pharmaceutical Premises Location, Inspection, Structure, Monitoring and Enforcement Regulations 2022 prescribe the requirements for the registration and location approval of pharmaceutical premises. According to the council, the regulations do not prohibit the registration of pharmaceutical premises in residential areas, provided the facilities meet the applicable statutory requirements. It added that whether a property designated for residential use could accommodate commercial pharmaceutical activities was not a determining factor in its assessment of applications for pharmaceutical location approval. The PCN consequently dismissed the allegation that it facilitated unlawful activities by registering the premises, describing it as unsubstantiated. On concerns about its enforcement capacity in Kano, the council explained that its regulatory framework operates through two established committees in every state: the Pharmaceutical Inspection Committee (PIC) and the Patent and Proprietary Medicines Vendors Licence Committee (PPMVLC). It said the committees are chaired by Directors of Pharmaceutical Services in the respective state ministries of health, with state chapters of the Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria providing additional representation. PCN officers serve as inspectors alongside other experienced pharmacists appointed to the committees, while the council’s state officer-in-charge serves as secretary and provides administrative support. The arrangement, it said, enables the council to mobilise sufficient personnel for regulatory activities, adding that its enforcement capacity should not be measured solely by the number of officers permanently stationed in a state. The council also cited the World Health Organisation’s Global Benchmarking assessment, which placed Nigeria at Maturity Level 3, as evidence of the country’s regulatory capacity. It said the PCN and NAFDAC remained the only national regulatory authorities in Africa to have attained and retained the global ranking. Pregabalin import licences Addressing the controversy surrounding pregabalin imports, the council clarified that issuing import licences to pharmaceutical importation companies fell within its statutory responsibilities, while NAFDAC was responsible for issuing product permits specifying the categories and quantities of products authorised for importation. It argued that the issuance of an import licence should not, in itself, be interpreted as evidence of wrongdoing, insisting that allegations of illegal distribution must be supported by evidence linking the products to specific violations. On the Coordinated Wholesale Centre (CWC), which featured prominently in the task force chairman’s allegations, the PCN said the initiative was developed by the Federal Government through the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare to address the proliferation of open drug markets. It explained that the initiative was designed to relocate identified and verified traders operating in open drug markets, including the Sabon Gari drug market in Kano, into a regulated wholesale environment. However, the council stressed that the CWC arrangement did not prohibit independent pharmaceutical wholesalers, distributors, importers and warehouse operators from establishing separate facilities for legitimate business activities. It therefore rejected the suggestion that registering an independent pharmaceutical premises outside the CWC amounted to undermining the objectives of the initiative. The council disclosed that CWC development was ongoing in Lagos, Anambra and Imo states, while Abia, Kaduna, Oyo and Gombe had secured approvals but were yet to commence construction. Challenges chairman to provide evidence On the allegation that some of its personnel were involved in illegal drug businesses, the PCN challenged Rimin-Gado to provide the names of the officials concerned, specific cases or other verifiable evidence to support his claims. It said it would not hesitate to investigate and sanction any staff member found culpable of misconduct, but cautioned against making sweeping allegations against public officials without evidence. The council also highlighted its monitoring framework for controlled medicines, disclosing that it had developed and deployed the Disposal of Poison Records, known as Form K, with support from the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), NAFDAC and other pharmaceutical stakeholders. Under the arrangement, it said all categories of pharmaceutical premises, including hospitals, were required to maintain records of controlled substances sold, distributed or dispensed. It added that facilities found negligent in maintaining the required records were liable to appropriate regulatory sanctions. Reaffirming its commitment to combating drug abuse and the unauthorised distribution of controlled medicines, the PCN said efforts to tackle illicit drugs required cooperation among regulatory agencies rather than institutional intimidation and unsubstantiated accusations. It urged the Kano task force chairman to submit any credible evidence of misconduct involving its personnel or registered pharmaceutical premises for investigation, insisting that it remained open to legitimate scrutiny. The council, however, warned that allegations capable of undermining public confidence in established regulatory institutions should not be made without verifiable facts. The post Kano drug war: PCN denies shielding illicit drug dealers appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: When grandpas, grandmas become cocaine smugglers
items.description: …404 ‘arrested’ in 20 months By Nnamdi Ojiego The image of an elderly grandmother or grandfather being led away by anti-narcotics officers over alleged involvement in drug trafficking is one that challenges conventional perceptions of who participates in the illicit drug trade. Yet, a succession of arrests involving people in their 60s, 70s and even older has brought an uncomfortable question to the fore: Why are people who should ordinarily be enjoying their retirement years becoming involved in the dangerous business of transporting, storing and distributing illicit drugs? In Nigeria, the figures supplied by Femi Babafemi, spokesperson of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) suggest that the phenomenon deserves closer attention. The agency arrested 240 persons aged 60 and above for drug-related offences in 2025, comprising 191 men and 49 women. Between January and August 2026, another 164 elderly suspects, including 128 men and 36 women, were arrested. The figures bring the total number of elderly persons arrested within the 20-month period to 404. Men accounted for the overwhelming majority, representing approximately 80 per cent of the arrests in 2025 and 78 per cent in the first eight months of 2026. Calculated strategy Although the 2026 figures cover only eight months and cannot be directly compared with the full-year 2025 total, the number of arrests already recorded points to the continued involvement of older people in drug-related activities. It also raises questions about the circumstances drawing them into a trade whose consequences include lengthy imprisonment, financial ruin, damaged family relationships and, in some cases, serious health risks. The NDLEA also reported seizing 6,998.77 kilogrammes of illicit drugs in connection with elderly suspects in 2025, compared with 1,479.988 kilogrammes between January and August 2026. From couriers to local dealers The cases recorded by the NDLEA in 2026 provide a glimpse into the different ways older people are becoming involved in the illicit drug trade. On March 14, 2026, NDLEA operatives arrested 74-year-old Ikwuakalom Nwakoro Emeka at the Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport, Abuja, while he was preparing to board a British Airways flight to London. The agency alleged that 11 kilogrammes of cocaine were discovered in his luggage, concealed in food items, including ground dry pepper. He reportedly told investigators he was travelling to Britain on holiday. Barely three months later, another high-profile case emerged at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos. On June 28, operatives arrested 67-year-old Mary Yetunde Barek, a Nigerian-British woman who worked as a caregiver in the United Kingdom, while she was preparing to board a Virgin Atlantic flight to London. The NDLEA alleged that 13 kilogrammes of cocaine were recovered from 31 large packages concealed in plantain peels designed to resemble actual plantain hands and packed among other food items. The agency reported that she admitted ownership of the drugs. However, she subsequently pleaded not guilty when arraigned, In April, the agency announced the arrest of 93-year-old Friday Ahukanna Chigbu at his residence in Abia State. A search of his home reportedly yielded 7.7 kilogrammes of skunk, a strain of cannabis. According to the NDLEA, the nonagenarian told investigators he had worked as a truck pusher before learning painting and tiling, but later entered the illicit drug business. He reportedly said he had been smoking skunk since 1959 before turning it into a business. Another striking case involved 101-year-old Esther Ogunmabo, arrested in Ilishan, Ogun State, on August 15, with 90 grammes of cannabis packaged in retail sachets. According to the agency, she told investigators that she turned to selling the substance after her provisions shop was destroyed by fire. She reportedly identified her daughter, who lives in Lagos, as the person arranging supplies every four days. These cases involve different substances and alleged roles. While Emeka and Barek were arrested over consignments of cocaine allegedly destined for the United Kingdom, Chigbu and Ogunmabo were accused of involvement in the local cannabis trade. They nevertheless expose a wider dimension of the problem: The involvement of older people is not confined to international drug smuggling. Some are being accused of retailing or keeping drugs within their communities, while others appear in investigations involving cross-border consignments. For security and criminal intelligence specialists, the development may reflect a calculated strategy by trafficking organisations that are increasingly willing to exploit age, social circumstances and public perceptions to move their consignments across borders. In this arrangement, elderly people may serve as couriers, carrying drugs in luggage or on their persons, while others may be used to store consignments or facilitate local distribution. Their involvement can range from deliberate participation for financial gain to alleged recruitment through deception, inducement or exploitation. The possibility that some elderly suspects are being recruited through personal connections also raises questions about the extent to which family members, friends and acquaintances may be involved in facilitating drug movements. Professor Al Chukwuma Okoli, a security governance expert at the Federal University of Lafia, believes trafficking networks are exploiting the assumptions society and security agencies sometimes make about older people. “The development points to the fact that trafficking networks are pragmatically exploiting demographic stereotypes,” he said. “Using elderly couriers guarantees them some measure of strategic cover because they (elderly persons) are perceived as low-risk entities who are less likely to attract routine security profiling at airports. This reveals a pattern of using vulnerable persons in order to circumvent law enforcement.” According to Okoli, older people experiencing financial difficulties arising from healthcare burdens and family pressures are among those traffickers may target. “The target population includes elderly persons who are undergoing financial difficulties owing to health burden, or family pressure. Traffickers usually identify and contact them through intimate local intermediaries, who advance them promises of significant gratification to secure their cooperation,” he said. His explanation suggests that recruitment may not always begin with strangers approaching elderly people at airports or offering them drugs directly. Instead, personal relationships and trusted intermediaries could provide traffickers with access to potential couriers, making it easier to persuade them to undertake risky assignments. For Alfred Ononugbo, a forensic investigator and criminal intelligence specialist, the circumstances surrounding such cases cannot be separated from the country’s weakening social protection system. He described social security as a foundation of governance and a necessary structure for protecting different categories of citizens, including the elderly, young people and working adults. “Social security welfare system is a trigger for governance. It is the bedrock on which democracy is built,” he said. According to him, a functional welfare system should provide social and economic protection that allows citizens to live with dignity, particularly after their productive years. “The welfare system did not compensate the elderly for their active years of service. They become vulnerable. “The government is disconnected from this special class of our society. There is no welfare programme by the government. I mean, look at the difficulty in accessing pensions and gratuity. These are factors that make these people a target. So criminals will offer them opportunities and incentives that probably will draw them out of their peaceful life in order to use them,” he said. Ononugbo also drew attention to the possible consequences of inadequate access to information and public enlightenment, particularly among older people who may not be familiar with the methods used by contemporary drug trafficking networks. “They don’t have information. They may not even be aware of narcotics, what it is. It’s not a common trend in their days,” he said. Ononugbo added that some older people might be struggling with the cost of healthcare, the welfare of their children and the loss of family members, leaving them open to approaches from people offering financial assistance or other incentives. He warned that the situation could worsen if government fails to address the social and economic conditions that leave older citizens exposed. “The elderly are vulnerable stage of the social entity called Nigeria. So they are vulnerable,” he said, arguing that the absence of adequate social and economic structures could push people seeking financial, emotional and social security towards the wrong sources of support. The business of recruiting grandparents Professor Okoli believes traffickers understand the social position of older people and may deliberately use it to their advantage. He said potential recruits are often identified through people already within their social circles, who can approach them with promises of substantial financial rewards. “Traffickers usually identify and contact them through intimate local intermediaries, who advance them promises of significant gratification to secure their cooperation,” he said. “Investigations often focus couriers. This is so because the courier is physically identifiable and detectable at the endpoint of the vicious chain of the drug dealing compartmentalisation,” he said. “The other actors, such as financiers and link persons, operate in the shadows of the opaque transactional jurisdictions, obviously making their attribution in the process harder and slower than the immediate arrest of the physically identifiable/detectable courier.” For Ononugbo, the handling of such investigations also deserves scrutiny. He expressed concern that suspects are sometimes publicly exposed before investigations have been concluded, warning that an arrest should not be confused with proof of guilt. “They have not been convicted by any competent court of any crime. So, but we have lost that,” he said. “In the West, they will take you to an isolation room and from there, interrogation will begin. But most often when suspects are apprehended at the airport, on the road, the next thing you see is the information gets online. At whatever stage, even with those items, they are considered as suspects by the law,” he added. The question of complicity The arrest of elderly travellers with large quantities of cocaine has also raised questions about the effectiveness of airport security and the possibility of internal collaboration in the movement of illicit drugs. Group Captain John Ojikutu (retd.), an aviation security expert and former commandant of the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos, argued that airports have several layers of passenger and baggage screening which, if properly implemented, should make it difficult for drug couriers to pass through undetected. He identified between six and eight layers of screening, beginning with intelligence gathering and passenger profiling before the issuance of tickets and continuing through check-in, departure terminals, immigration and security checks, boarding gates and baggage screening. According to him, airlines are expected to use Computer Assisted Passenger Screening Systems (CAPPS) to identify passengers who may pose security risks or threats. Passengers identified as requiring enhanced screening should be subjected to additional checks, while those considered serious threats may be placed on no-fly lists. He questioned whether airlines and other relevant authorities consistently apply these procedures before allowing passengers to proceed with their journeys. “There are about six to eight layers for the screening of passengers,” Ojikutu said, explaining that the process should involve intelligence sharing among relevant authorities, airlines, aviation regulators and airport security operators. He said passengers undergo further checks at the airline check-in counters, where checked-in luggage is screened before boarding passes are issued. “Additional screening follows at the passenger holding terminal, while immigration and state security personnel conduct further checks before the final boarding process. Checked-in baggage also undergoes another screening at the baggage screening hall without the passenger being present. “If these are done with the sincerity of purpose, most of the free access for air drug traffickers will be closed except where there are accomplices at the aviation-airport security/defence layers,” he said. Ojikutu stressed that age should not exempt any passenger from security screening, arguing that the same risk assessment principles should apply to elderly travellers, younger passengers and even flight crew. “Nobody is exempted from security profiling except the President or Head of State of the aircraft originating country,” he said. He added that screening machines and sniffer dogs are deployed at airports to detect prohibited substances and other security threats, depending on the risk assessment and security programmes of individual airports. items.title: Turkish, Azeri, SCO officials arrive in Islamabad for ECO ministerial
items.description: Foreign dignitaries continue to arrive in Islamabad as the capital gears up to host the two-day 30th meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organisation (ECO) Council of Ministers starting today. Among the visiting dignitaries is Turkish Deputy Foreign Minister Musa Kulaklikaya, who was received by Foreign Office (FO) officials upon his arrival, the FO said on Sunday. Azeri Deputy Foreign Minister Elnur Mammadov and Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Deputy Secretary General Ahmad Saidmurodzoda are also among those who have reached Islamabad for the meeting. On Saturday, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus Tahsin Ertugruloglu also arrived in Islamabad to participate in the meeting. The ECO’s ministerial meeting will be chaired by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and attended by foreign ministers and heads of delegations from ECO member states, along with representatives of the organisation’s secretariat and subsidiary bodies. It will be preceded by a gathering of senior officials from ECO member states, who will review the organisation’s activities and programmes, assess the work of its subsidiary bodies and finalise the agenda and draft outcome documents for consideration by the ministers. Pakistan, which holds the ECO chairmanship for 2026-27, will seek to advance the organisation’s objectives under the theme “Reviving Regionalism for a Resilient ECO”, the FO said in a statement on Saturday. It said Pakistan’s chairmanship would focus on strengthening regional connectivity and integration, deepening partnerships and promoting collective efforts for economic prosperity and sustainable development. The chairmanship would also provide an opportunity to strengthen the ECO’s role as a platform for regional cooperation, dialogue and economic collaboration, it added. According to the FO, Pakistan also aims to position itself as a regional connectivity hub, facilitate logistics supply chains and help shape the agenda for regional trade. The efforts would help unlock the region’s economic potential and translate the benefits of regional cooperation into tangible improvements in the lives of people in ECO member states, the statement said. Currently, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Tajikistan, Iran, Turkiye, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyz Republic and Uzbekistan are part of the ECO.

items.description: …Report says 640 killed in October as a result of broader insecurity …Experts warn against violence, fake news By Nnamdi Ojiego 60 days to the 2027 general elections, concerns are mounting over the safety of the electoral process as rising insecurity, attacks on political gatherings and the spread of misinformation threaten to undermine citizens’ participation in the polls. The concerns have been heightened by fresh incidents of political violence in different parts of the country, including Calabar, Cross River State, Asaba, Delta State, and Sokoto, where political supporters and opposition figures have reportedly come under attack. The developments have renewed questions about the preparedness of security agencies to protect candidates, party supporters and voters, particularly in a country already grappling with banditry, insurgency, kidnapping and communal violence. A report by the Centre for Democracy and Development (CDD), Nigeria Election Security Tracker for October 2026 provides a troubling picture of the security situation. It recorded 640 deaths during the month (October), representing a 61.62 per cent increase from the 396 deaths recorded in September. Of the 640 deaths, 638 were attributed to broader insecurity, while two resulted from election-related attacks in Enugu and Ebonyi. The North-East accounted for the highest number of fatalities, with 409 deaths. The report also documented 16 election-related incidents in October, compared with 14 in September, representing a 14.29 per cent increase. Attacks on campaign gatherings and convoys accounted for 11 of the 16 incidents. Other cases involved assaults on individuals, attacks on political property and the restriction of a political gathering. The incidents affected several political parties, including the All Progressives Congress (APC) and African Democratic Congress (ADC), which each recorded four cases, while the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) recorded three. Two of the incidents were fatal. Ifeanyi Nwolie died from gunshot injuries sustained during the NDC campaign launch in Enugu on October 10. In Ebonyi, gunmen attacked the convoy of NDC candidate, Rollins Offia-Nwali, on October 22, killing one person, injuring three others and burning his vehicle. The candidate reportedly escaped. The CDD report also documented attacks on ADC convoys in Igueben and Kogi, disruption of PDP consultations in Calabar, an attack on an ADC candidate’s meeting in Obosi, Anambra State, and the prevention of supporters from gathering for the Obi-Kwankwaso march in Abuja. Although broader insecurity accounted for most of the fatalities, the report warned that its consequences could extend to the electoral process, particularly in communities where residents have been displaced or roads have become unsafe. According to the report, insecurity could prevent election officials and party agents from reaching vulnerable communities, while displaced residents and those living in unsafe areas may be unable to check the voter register or reach their polling centres. November incidents heighten concerns Developments in November appear to have reinforced the concerns raised by the October report. In Calabar, Cross River State, the convoy of Peter Obi, presidential candidate of the NDC, and party supporters reportedly came under attack by suspected political thugs on November 4, shortly after his arrival in the state capital for a political engagement. The attackers allegedly hurled stones, bottles and other dangerous objects at the convoy around Watt Market, leaving several supporters injured and vehicles damaged. The police confirmed the incident and announced the arrest of a 27-year-old suspect, while investigations commenced to identify other suspects and their alleged sponsors. On the same day, police intervened to prevent a possible confrontation between NDC supporters attending Obi’s town hall meeting and APC supporters holding a rally in another part of Calabar. The two groups reportedly converged around the Metropolitan Hotel area, disrupting movement and commercial activities before security operatives restored order. In Asaba, Delta State, the situation was more tragic. A political procession organised by the Obidient/OK Movement in support of the NDC presidential candidate was attacked by suspected hoodlums along Nnebisi Road on November 7. One person was killed and five others injured, according to the Delta State Police Command. The police said they had received intelligence indicating the possibility of violence and had advised the organisers against an open-road procession, recommending a designated venue where adequate security could be provided. The organisers, however, proceeded with the procession, according to the police account. The incident generated accusations and counter-accusations between the NDC and APC. While NDC chieftain and former Speaker of the Delta State House of Assembly, Victor Ochei, accused members of the ruling party of being responsible, the APC denied the allegation, insisting that there was no evidence linking its members to the violence. Police said investigations were ongoing. In Sokoto, the ADC raised the alarm over alleged attacks on its supporters, including members of its women’s wing who participated in a solidarity march on October 28. The party also alleged that its governorship candidate, Manir Muhammad Dan’iya, survived a gun attack on his convoy at the Sultan Abubakar III International Airport on October 30. It accused suspected gunmen and alleged involvement of state-owned security outfits. The party further alleged that its campaign office was attacked and that its planned activities were being frustrated through intimidation and pressure on hotel operators. The November developments have raised fresh concerns about the ability of political parties to conduct their activities without intimidation and the capacity of security agencies to guarantee the safety of all contestants and their supporters. Misinformation, another threat to 2027 Beyond physical attacks and insecurity, the CDD report identified misinformation, disinformation and hate speech as additional threats to the electoral environment. It recorded 75 misinformation, disinformation and hate speech narratives in October, down from 105 in September. Of the October narratives, 37 were false, 31 were misleading, two involved religious threats and hostility, while five could neither be confirmed nor disproved with available evidence. Some of the claims involved fabricated quotations and manipulated images targeting political candidates, while recycled videos were circulated to exaggerate political support. The report also identified AI-generated images falsely portraying former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and Aminu Tambuwal as receiving Bello Turji into the ADC. Other fabricated images falsely suggested that campaign materials had been damaged by supporters following an APC rally in Kaduna. False voter registration information and fabricated candidate notices also circulated, with some using INEC’s identity to mislead the public. The CDD warned that such narratives could undermine public confidence in electoral institutions and create confusion among voters, particularly when false information circulates alongside genuine administrative challenges. ‘Nobody should risk life to attend rally or vote’ Commenting on the implications of the findings, Dengiyefa Angalapu, CDD’s Research Analyst, said the most significant development in October was the increase in the lethality of security incidents. According to him, the average number of reported deaths per incident more than doubled, with broader insecurity accounting for 638 of the 640 fatalities. He said the Binnari attack in Taraba State, which claimed 62 lives and displaced more than 5,000 people, illustrated the severity of the situation. Angalapu cautioned against assessing the country’s security situation solely through the number of recorded incidents, stressing that the consequences of attacks on communities could extend to the electoral process. “The big change was how deadly October’s incidents were. Average reported deaths per incident more than doubled, with broader insecurity accounting for 638 of the 640 deaths. That includes community attacks and deaths reported in military operations,” he said. He added that displacement and unsafe roads could prevent eligible voters from checking the register or reaching polling units, while also making it difficult for INEC officials to access affected communities. Describing the situation as an early warning requiring urgent attention, Angalapu said the two deaths recorded in campaign attacks in October were only part of the wider threat to political participation. “Two people were killed in campaign attacks in October, and intimidation can keep many more away from politics. We need police protection for every party, including the roads supporters use, and a quick response to threats,” he said. He called for sustained investigations into political attacks, prosecution of suspects where evidence supports charges and greater responsibility from political party leaders. “Party leaders must also rein in members who encourage violence, while INEC needs practical arrangements for displaced voters and unsafe communities. Nobody should have to risk their life to attend a rally or cast a vote,” he added. ‘Electoral process inexorably bound to be violent’ For Sylvester Akhaine, Professor of Political Science at Lagos State University, the growing incidence of political violence must be examined against the background of Nigeria’s troubled party politics and the struggle for political power. He argued that the problem begins with the process through which political parties select candidates, noting that the absence of genuine internal democracy contributes to the emergence of contestants whose political ambitions are driven largely by the pursuit of power and personal accumulation. “Electoral integrity begins from the choice of contestants to run for public office. Do they emanate from a process underlined by internal party democracy? In our context, these processes are fraught with manipulation. Elements without character are thrown up for electoral contests,” he said. Akhaine argued that where politics becomes the primary means of economic accumulation, competition for political office is likely to become fierce and violent. “Against the backdrop of politics as the only game in town and primary source of easy accumulation, the process is inexorably bound to be violent. The present contestants in the field are all over-ambitious elements, hence the incremental violence being encountered,” he added. On the implications for voter participation, the political scientist warned that an atmosphere of insecurity could affect turnout and ultimately influence electoral outcomes. “In an atmosphere of siege, it is bound to affect the turnout of voters. Fear and violence would affect electoral outcomes,” he said. He maintained that the attacks reflected a history of violence that had continued to dog Nigeria’s electoral process, arguing that institutional reforms alone might not be sufficient without a change in the character and disposition of those occupying positions of authority. “Institutions are habituated by men and women. The beautiful ones have not been born. Enlightened self-interest might save the day,” he said. ‘Security agencies overstretched’ A security governance expert at the Federal University of Lafia, Professor Al Chukwuma Okoli, also expressed concern over the increasing lethality of insecurity, warning that the security situation could make the 2027 electoral process more difficult to manage. He said the sharp rise in fatalities, despite the relatively modest increase in election-related incidents, suggested that insecurity was becoming more deadly and unpredictable. According to him, the security challenges require a shift from reactive deployments to intelligence-led operations, with stronger coordination among security agencies. “The spike in human fatalities relative to what seems to be a modest rise in election-related incidents suggests that insecurity is becoming more lethal and less predictable. This implies, among other things, that securing 2027 election requires proactive, intelligence-focused and synergised security approach instead of a reactive and often uncoordinated deployment of forces,” he said. Okoli noted that security agencies were already overstretched in several parts of the country affected by banditry, terrorism and other forms of armed violence. He warned that this could leave campaign convoys and political gatherings vulnerable, particularly where there was inadequate intelligence gathering, early warning and coordination. He therefore urged federal and state authorities to conduct threat assessments before political events, secure campaign routes and establish rapid response mechanisms. “State and Federal authorities should put in place measures that are amenable to pre-event threat assessments. This is in addition to ensuring secured and varied convoy routes, rapid response mechanisms, protected polling and collation arenas, and clear safety communication for both the voting populace and other political actors,” he said. A forensic investigator and criminal intelligence specialist, Alfred Ononugbo, was less optimistic about the ability of security agencies to contain the situation, arguing that the country’s wider governance and economic challenges could affect their effectiveness. He suggested that politically motivated intimidation and violence were becoming part of the struggle for political advantage ahead of the elections. According to him, the situation could worsen if political actors continue to resort to intimidation rather than presenting their records and programmes to voters. “If you are running a performance-based campaign, you will not necessarily need these unauthorised activities and subterranean activities of anti-social people,” he said. Ononugbo also expressed concern that security personnel, being Nigerians themselves, were not insulated from the economic difficulties affecting the country. He argued that poor remuneration, rising living costs and other economic pressures could expose security operatives to undue influence from powerful political interests. “You see, when you talk of Nigerian security agencies, you forget that they are Nigerians and victims of the same poor performance of governance. So you don’t expect anything fantastic from people who are saddled with all manner of burdens that is weighing them down,” he said. He warned that security agencies were already grappling with terrorism and banditry, and the addition of politically motivated violence could further stretch their capacity. “The police and the security agencies are overwhelmed. They are dealing with the terrorism and banditry. Now you are bringing political violence to add to their overwhelmed,” he said. Ononugbo called for widespread civic education and public awareness to help Nigerians understand that their votes and democratic choices belonged to them and must be protected. He urged the media, civil society groups and other stakeholders to take a more active role in educating citizens and discouraging political violence. ‘INEC must map risk-prone areas’ A former spokesperson for the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Barrister Fetus Okoye, said the commission must work closely with security agencies to protect election officials, voters and other stakeholders, particularly in areas prone to violence. He said the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security must be fully engaged to ensure adequate security arrangements before and during elections. According to him, the Police Force remains the lead agency for election security and should coordinate the deployment of other security agencies. “The Commission must map the country using its Risk Management Tool (ERM) and Election Violence Mitigation and Advocacy Tool (EVMAT) to help security agencies deploy effectively in risk-prone areas,” he said. Warning that insecurity could discourage citizens from participating in the electoral process, Okoye said: “Nigerians will disengage from the electoral process if the electoral environment is too toxic. Elections should be a festival of democracy, not a dance of death.” On the situation of internally displaced persons (IDPs), he said Section 24 of the Electoral Act provides for measures to prevent people displaced by emergencies from being disenfranchised, as far as practicable. He added that INEC already had a framework for voting by IDPs, which should be effectively implemented where necessary. The former INEC spokesperson also insisted that conducting a successful election required the cooperation of political parties, security agencies and other stakeholders. “Conducting and delivering a successful election is a multi-stakeholder effort. No single entity, including the Commission, can deliver a successful election without the input, cooperation, and understanding of political parties and security agencies. “The Commission does not use violence or train and employ political thugs. It does not create a toxic electoral environment. Political parties in Nigeria do not seem to learn from history, in which violence and electoral malfeasance collapsed previous democratic regimes,” he said. Okoye further advocated the establishment of a Political Parties Regulation and Electoral Offences Commission to regulate political parties and investigate, arrest and prosecute electoral offenders. He said INEC itself must remain transparent, courageous and politically neutral in the discharge of its responsibilities, treating all parties and competing interests equally. ‘Culture of impunity laying foundation for chaos’ Rev. Fr. Atta Barkindo, Executive Director of The Kukah Centre, expressed concern that repeated violations of the peace accord, Electoral Act and Constitution by political actors could lay the foundation for chaos ahead of the elections. He said the National Peace Committee (NPC) was particularly worried about the apparent absence of consequences for political actors who disregard agreed rules and democratic conventions. “First, Nigerians are seeing for themselves the attitude of politicians, parties, and party spokespersons. The NPC is very concerned that the ongoing violations of the peace accord, the Electoral Act and even the Constitution is laying the foundation for chaos,” he said. “It is even more concerning that the culture of impunity is deepening in all ramifications without consequences,” he added. Barkindo said the committee was preparing to engage relevant stakeholders and urge them to exercise restraint and comply with the rules governing political activities. However, he stressed that the committee’s influence was largely moral and that the responsibility for enforcing the law rested with institutions constitutionally empowered and funded by taxpayers. “The NPC can only deploy its moral voice. It is beholden on those whose responsibility is backed up by the Constitution and paid by taxpayers to live up to their responsibilities,” he said. He urged politicians to resist the temptation to pursue electoral victory at all costs, warning that the country’s stability should not be sacrificed for individual political ambitions. “The politicians should not be blinded by the unbridled desire to win at all cost at the detriment of the country,” he said. The problem, therefore, extends beyond the physical security of polling centres. Voters also need reliable information to make informed decisions and participate meaningfully in the electoral process. Vanguard Newspaper The post 60 DAYS TO POLLS: Fear over electoral process as political attacks rise appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Umahi gives directors three weeks to make highways motorable
items.description: By John Alechenu Minister of Works, David Umahi, has given Zonal Directors of the ministry three weeks to make major federal highways motorable ahead of the festive season. Umahi gave the directive at a meeting with Coordinating Directors of Highways Construction and Rehabilitation, Bridges and Design, and Zonal Directors in Abuja. A statement issued on Saturday by the ministry’s Director of Information and Public Relations, Mohammed Ahmed, quoted the minister as saying that making roads motorable must take priority over permanent construction. “Nigerians are about to travel for the festive season. Roads cannot remain impassable while contractors chase long-term targets,” the statement said. Umahi warned that contractors would no longer be allowed to concentrate on permanent construction while other sections of the same roads remained inaccessible. He directed the Zonal Directors to return to project sites immediately and ensure that failed sections were repaired through pothole filling, application of sharp sand, stone base, cement stabilisation, binder and wearing courses, depending on the condition of the roads. Among the roads listed for urgent attention were Zaria-Funtua-Gusau-Sokoto, Mararaba-Keffi, Abuja-Lokoja, Kano-Katsina, Keffi-Makurdi, Makurdi-Enugu, East-West Road, Benin Bypass, Benin-Warri, Benin-Asaba, Warri-Oleh, Kano-Shuwarin and Bauchi-Gombe. Others in the South-East included Enugu-Port Harcourt, Enugu-Aba, Abakaliki-Enugu, Abakaliki-Gojia and Aba-Port Harcourt. The minister directed contractors handling the projects to cooperate with ministry officials and carry out the remedial works, warning that any contractor whose activities compromised road users’ safety would be reported for appropriate action. He also ordered Zonal Directors to personally inspect projects and submit detailed reports on road conditions, work done, challenges, contractors’ commitments and required interventions. For effective monitoring, he directed the establishment of a dedicated WhatsApp platform through which reports would be submitted, indicating responsible officers, project locations, contractors, challenges and recommendations. Umahi announced that he would begin visiting the zones from Monday to assess compliance and evaluate the performance of directors and supervising officers. The post Umahi gives directors three weeks to make highways motorable appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Christian persecution in Nigeria worrisome — Catholic bishops
items.description: By Chidi Nkwopara Church leaders have expressed concern over the increasing cases of violent persecution of Christians in parts of Nigeria, saying the disturbing trend has worsened over the past two decades. The Apostolic Nuncio to Nigeria, Archbishop Michael Francis Crotty, and the Archbishop of Owerri, Most Rev. Lucius Iwejuru Ugorji, raised the concern at the weekend in Owerri during their respective addresses at the 18th National Conference of the Association of Papal Knights and Medalists in Nigeria (APKMN). In his address, Crotty said Christians had suffered persecution in different forms throughout Nigeria’s history, but noted that violent forms of persecution had become more pronounced in the last two decades. “In the history of Nigeria, Christians have suffered persecution in different forms, and this disturbing phenomenon has increased within the last two decades, especially the violent forms of persecution. “In recent years, Christians have been targeted by kidnappers, and many lay faithful and priests have been kidnapped. “Many of those kidnapped were killed, and others were released after ransoms were paid. Thousands of churches have been attacked and destroyed since the beginning of Boko Haram and the activities of herdsmen in more recent years,” he said. The Apostolic Nuncio also alleged that Christians in some parts of the country, particularly the North and North-Central regions, had been denied legitimate access to land for the construction of places of worship. “Very often the issue of persecution of Christians in Nigeria is politicised and approached with some sort of bias and religious sentiments. “There is no doubt that people of other faiths have also been affected by insecurity in Nigeria. However, we cannot deny the fact that Christians have been specifically targeted in some parts of the country. “Our concern should be the necessary actions to take in order to bring the unnecessary killing of all citizens to an end, whether they are Christian or of other faiths,” he said. He described the conference theme, “Strategic Engagements in Addressing Christian Persecution in Nigeria: Toward Coordinated Response”, as timely, stressing the need for collective action across religious and community lines. In his address, Archbishop Ugorji said the human and material consequences of the country’s insecurity remained alarming, irrespective of whether the crisis was viewed as targeted persecution of Christians or a complex socio-economic conflict. “Ultimately, whether the crisis is perceived as a targeted persecution of Christians or a complex socio-economic conflict, the human and material toll is undeniable. “It is deeply troubling that tens of thousands have lost their lives, millions remain internally displaced, the education of thousands of children is truncated, and millions of naira have been lost through destruction of property and paying ransom,” he said. Ugorji called on the government to strengthen its responsibility to protect citizens and hold perpetrators of violence accountable, irrespective of their religious affiliations. “We have to state loud and clear that it is the responsibility of government to prevent human rights violations, protect vulnerable populations, whether they are Christians or Muslims, and ensure accountability for crimes against law-abiding citizens.” The post Christian persecution in Nigeria worrisome — Catholic bishops appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: 2027: Abuja natives reject anti-Tinubu protest
items.description: By Omeiza Ajayi Natives and residents of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) have rejected the protest against President Bola Tinubu at a mosque in Abuja, describing the demonstrators as outsiders and pledging to mobilise 65 per cent of the territory’s votes for him in the 2027 general elections. The ‘Supreme Leader’ of FCT Youths, Ambassador Isaac David, told Sunday Vanguard that the protesters did not represent the indigenous people of the territory. He was reacting to the incident at the Shehu Shagari Central Mosque, Area 1, Garki, Abuja, where the President attended Friday prayers on November 13. David said: “Those individuals do not represent FCT natives, they do not represent FCT youths, and they certainly do not speak for the genuine voters of the territory. “Information available to us indicates that they were brought into the FCT from different states following the announcement that Mr President would observe Friday prayers at the mosque. We believe they were sponsored to create negative publicity, mislead Nigerians and portray the President as unpopular.” Tinubu reportedly encountered a hostile reception from some worshippers and youths who booed him and chanted slogans, including “Tinubu Must Go”, “Ba ma so” and “Ba ma yi”, as his convoy departed the mosque. The incident attracted widespread attention after videos of the protest circulated on social media. There were also reports that some individuals threw objects at the presidential convoy, although the Presidency disputed claims surrounding the alleged attack. David accused opposition political interests of sponsoring the mobilisation to create an impression of widespread rejection of the President and generate material for negative political campaigns. He argued that the interests and political aspirations of the territory’s original inhabitants could not be determined by individuals allegedly mobilised from outside the FCT. “The opposition wants to exploit this incident for cheap political advantage. Their intention is to deceive Nigerians, gain popularity on social media and discredit the good work of President Tinubu through the Honourable Minister of the FCT, Chief Nyesom Wike. “They also want to portray the minister as someone who has done nothing for the territory and cannot fulfil his promises. We reject that narrative. The actions of a few individuals cannot erase the realities of development in our communities or determine the position of the original inhabitants,” he said. The post 2027: Abuja natives reject anti-Tinubu protest appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Why Edo was among first states to approve state police — Okpebholo
items.description: By Ozioruva Aliu THE governor of Edo, Senator Monday Okpebholo, has said the state already has the structure for state police to commence and for that reason, the state House of Assembly was one of the first to pass the law as recommended by the National Assembly. Okpebholo spoke in an interview with journalists in Benin-City as part of activities to mark his second year anniversary. “We are prepared. We were one of the first to sign into law, when others were talking, we said no, it is working for us and right now, to be honest with you, even with our vigilantes, we already have state police because it is working for us. Edo state is safe.” He said his state already has a working security architecture it has tested that could be used to track criminals even outside the state,” he said. Okpebholo said “Remember there was this kidnapping that happened and within 24 hours which has never happened in Nigeria, we got the guys, so that is it. We are prepared to go to other states when they take any of our citizens. We did it in Kogi, then something happened in Ogun, I called the governor, I said, please, I don’t want my person to stay with this kidnapper for more than five days and as God would have it, he was able to get them out within a short time. So somebody has to be prudent with everything.” On security in the state, Governor Okpebholo said his administration took stiff measures to reduce the level of killings and kidnapping in the state. Some of the measures, he said, was destroying any building that was linked to kidnapping and cult related activities in the state irrespective of the social status of the person involved. He said: “These are stiff measures we have taken that are really working for us. To be honest with you, if not that we have done that, maybe you won’t be able to stay in Benin for two nights. Today nightlife is back, business is booming at night, even supermarkets are beginning to open at night. “In the next few weeks, it will be safer because there will be police at every corner of the state to watch everyone. They will be equipped even with motorbikes so that when somebody thinks he can run, then they will follow the person. Whether you take a bush path, they will follow you up.” The post Why Edo was among first states to approve state police — Okpebholo appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Yari to critics: You did nothing about insecurity for 20 yrs
items.description: …Says, FAAC allocations now in trillions By Omeiza Ajayi The Director General of the All Progressives Congress Presidential Campaign Council APC-PCC, Senator Abdulaziz Yari, has told those saying the party has no plan for security that they did nothing about insecurity in 20 years. He spoke on Saturday at the APC presidential rally in Jos, the Plateau State capital. “Those who are saying we don’t have plan for security, I want to remind them that they did nothing about insecurity for over 20 years about it because it started during their time,” Yari said. According to him, the APC will implement its manifesto to the letter, promising that by 2031 almost everything promised would have been achieved. Yari told the gathering that Plateau’s political players had come out to assure the President of the state’s votes in the 2027 general election. “The key players, active players in the Plateau politics are all here before you to give you the assurances that 2027 Plateau is 101% assured,” he said. He described Tinubu as “the person that met the federation account of Nigeria as at June 2023 at N732 billion. But today, we thank God, Mr President, we thank you for your hard work and your special leadership. We are now counting the federation account in trillions.” The post Yari to critics: You did nothing about insecurity for 20 yrs appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: HERBERT MACAULAY@162: Nigeria’s devt doomed until we end primitive leadership selection — Jonathan
items.description: …Macaulay’s legacy inspires my education, skills devt agenda – Tinubu …Sanwo-Olu, Osuntokun, Jinadu, Osaghae, Arogundade speak …Bode George asks Tinubu to return Macaulay’s demolished ancestral home By Clifford Ndujihe, Dapo Akinrefon & Henry Obetta LAGOS – From the lips of eminent Nigerians including political leaders and scholars, it was an ocean tributes, yesterday, for late elder statesman and father of Nigeria’s nationalism, Sir Herbert Macaulay, who posthumously turned 162 years. Speaking at a memorial colloquium organised by the Macaulay Heritage Foundation, speaker after speaker urged leaders to imbibe the political and leadership virtues of Macaulay to fast track Nigeria’s development. This was as the organisers urged the Federal Government to return the land where the General Post Office, Lagos, is built to the Macaulay to be turned into a site to house Macaulay’s monuments and legacies for future generation to learn from. It’s time to end poor leadership selection process Former President Goodluck Jonathan, who chaired the event warned that Nigeria will continue to struggle with development unless it abandons what he described as primitive methods of selecting political leaders based on religion, ethnicity, language and other narrow considerations. He urged Nigerians to prioritise competence and merit in leadership recruitment, arguing that the country’s enormous human and natural resources would remain underutilised if political choices continued to be driven by primordial sentiments. The colloquium, themed Nationalism and Nation Building, attracted prominent political leaders, academics, professionals and other stakeholders, including President Bola Tinubu, who was represented by the Deputy Vice Chancellor of University of Lagos, Professor Afolabi Leshi; Lagos Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu, former Minister of External Affairs, General Ike Nwachukwu, retd; former Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, Deputy National Chairman, Chief Olabode George; Emeritus Professor Jide Osuntokun; Professor Adele Jinadu; and Director-General of the Nigerian Institute of International Affairs, NIIA, Professor Eghosa Osaghae. Jonathan identified leadership failures, institutional weaknesses, corruption, policy inconsistency, inadequate infrastructure, insecurity and over-dependence on raw material exports as major obstacles to Nigeria’s development. He also called for comprehensive democratic reforms, functional education, research-driven universities, stronger institutions and a national development agenda anchored on measurable targets and accountability. Describing Nigeria’s democratic system as “opaque and amorphous”, he said it must be restructured to guarantee popular participation, the rule of law, respect for human rights, judicial independence, accountability, pluralism and a vibrant civil society. Paying tribute to Macaulay, whom he described as a man of remarkable intellect, courage and conviction, Jonathan said the nationalist’s struggle went beyond the transfer of political power from colonial authorities to Nigerians. He said: “Herbert Macaulay was a man of remarkable intellect, courage and conviction. An engineer, journalist, political activist and public intellectual, he distinguished himself as one of the earliest voices to challenge colonial injustice and demand greater political participation and self-determination for Nigerians. Tinubu, Sanwo-Olu pay tributes President Bola Tinubu, represented by the Deputy Vice-Chancellor of the University of Lagos, Professor Foluso Afolabi Lesi, described Macaulay as a visionary leader, patriot and fearless advocate of justice and self-determination. He said education remained one of the greatest ways to preserve the nationalist’s legacy, noting that the Federal Government was implementing reforms to improve access to quality education, strengthen skills development and promote innovation under the Renewed Hope Agenda. The President cited the Nigerian Education Loan Fund, NELFUND, skills development initiatives and start-up grants for young entrepreneurs as interventions aimed at preparing Nigerian youths for the global economy. Tinubu commended the Macaulay family, George and the foundation for preserving the nationalist’s memory, urging Nigerians to emulate his integrity, courage and selfless service. Governor Sanwo-Olu, represented by the Secretary to the State Government, Mrs Abimbola Salu-Hundeyin, reaffirmed Lagos State’s commitment to collaborating with the foundation to preserve Macaulay’s legacy. The governor, who received the Herbert Macaulay Award for Leadership in Public Service, Cultural Ambassadorship and Urban Development, said his administration had pursued improvements in transportation, infrastructure, public institutions and opportunities for Lagos residents. He said the state was committed to modernising Lagos without losing its historical identity and cultural character. The President of the Nigerian Society of Engineers, Engr. Ali Alimasuya Rabiu, represented by Engr. Ayotunde Olukayode Ogunnoiki, also described Macaulay as Nigeria’s first indigenous professional engineer and one of the foremost pioneers of Nigerian nationalism. He said the country needed the vision, courage, intellectual rigour and commitment to public service that characterised Macaulay’s life. Macaulay, born on November 14, 1864, is widely regarded as the father of Nigerian nationalism. He died in Kano in 1946, 14 years before Nigeria attained independence. 2060: What kind of country will we celebrate? Expressing concern over Nigeria’s development trajectory, Jonathan challenged the country to examine its performance against the aspirations of the founding nationalists. He compared Nigeria’s development with that of South Korea, India and Singapore, which gained independence or emerged from colonial rule around the same period but had recorded remarkable advances in industrialisation, technology, education, healthcare and human development. He said South Korea had become a global force in electronics and advanced manufacturing, Singapore a major centre of global commerce and innovation, while India had established itself in technology and healthcare. “Where is Nigeria and African countries in comparison? What has prevented us from translating our enormous human and natural resources into comparable levels of development? What are the stumbling blocks that have kept us from realising a greater percentage of the aspirations that inspired our independence?” he asked. He noted that Nigeria would mark the centenary of its independence in 2060, just 34 years away, and urged leaders to begin preparing for that milestone. “The question is: what kind of country will we be celebrating in 2060? “Will we have overcome the challenges confronting us today, or will another generation be lamenting the same failures and unrealised aspirations? “Where will Nigeria stand in the Human Development Index? What will be our life expectancy, the quality of our education and healthcare, and the standard of living of the average Nigerian? What progress will we have made in science, technology, digital innovation and industrial development?” he asked. The former President said these questions must form the basis of a national development agenda with clear objectives, measurable targets, timelines and identifiable responsibilities. He added: “Our political leaders must provide direction in line with a well-established national vision; our public institutions must deliver efficiently; our businesses must invest in productive capacity; our educational institutions must prepare our people for the demands of the future; and our citizens must embrace the values of hard work, integrity, patriotism and responsible citizenship.” Jonathan also urged young Nigerians to take responsibility for advancing the ideals of nationalism through innovation, enterprise, civic participation and accountability. He said: “We must not allow Herbert Macaulay, Nnamdi Azikiwe, Obafemi Awolowo, Ahmadu Bello and the other founding nationalists regret, even in their graves, the struggle they waged for our independence. “The present generation must therefore resolve that the lamentations of today will not become the inheritance of our children and grandchildren. The greatest tribute to our national heroes is not merely to celebrate their birthdays or preserve their monuments, but to build a nation that reflects the ideals for which they struggled.” Jinadu, Osaghae, Arogundade demand reforms In separate interventions, prominent scholars and public intellectuals called for a fundamental reorientation of Nigeria’s political and governance systems, insisting that the ideals represented by Macaulay remained relevant to the country’s development challenges. Professor Adele Jinadu said the nationalist represented the courage of intellectuals and professionals to speak truth to power, a quality he regretted was increasingly missing in Nigeria. He lamented that the professional and middle classes had largely remained silent in the face of democratic backsliding because of ethnic considerations and the politics of whose turn it was to produce the President. “We are all quiet in the face of the backslide that we are going through, almost going to the precipice. We have turned those who should not be heroes into heroes. And those who should be heroes, we don’t celebrate them,” he said. Jinadu argued that Nigerians should assess political leaders based on competence rather than ethnicity, adding that the middle class had a responsibility to lead the struggle against democratic decline. He also recalled Macaulay’s contribution to the nationalist movement and regretted that his death in 1946 interrupted the political mobilisation that could have helped build a broader national political movement. On his part, Professor Osaghae, Director-General of the NIIA, said Macaulay distinguished himself from a middle class increasingly given to consumerism and conspicuous consumption. He highlighted the cosmopolitan character of colonial Lagos and its contribution to the emergence of Pan-African nationalism, arguing that Nigeria must continually fine-tune its federal arrangement to accommodate the country’s diversity. Osaghae said federalism was a continuing process that must respond to changing political realities and accommodate different groups without undermining national unity. He cited the Nigerian National Democratic Party, NNDP, and the National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons, NCNC, as examples of political movements that brought together diverse interests. Media rights activist, Lanre Arogundade, outlined six lessons from Macaulay’s nationalism that Nigeria must embrace to build a just and prosperous society. They included a non-parasitic ruling class, protection of citizens from oppressive taxation and impoverishing policies, universal education, freedom of expression, people-oriented political parties and rejection of tribalism. He argued that public office should be about service rather than personal enrichment, noting that Macaulay earned his living through his professional practice as an engineer and surveyor. Arogundade also condemned growing intolerance of criticism, warning that democracy could not survive where citizens and journalists were denied the freedom to question those in power. He called for a national memorial to Macaulay, suggesting that Lagos State should establish one at CMS Grammar School, and advocated a wider programme of activities to teach younger generations about the nationalist’s contributions. Bode George seeks return of Macaulay’s house Earlier, Chief Olabode George, a grand-nephew of Macaulay, appealed to President Tinubu to return the nationalist’s demolished ancestral home to his descendants for conversion into a permanent memorial centre. George recalled that the colonial authorities demolished the house shortly after Macaulay’s death in 1946 and built the General Post Office on the site. He said the family was prepared to establish a memorial hall where younger generations could learn about the nationalist’s contributions to Nigeria’s political development. “We are Nigerians. We must be proud of those God has given us,” he said. He added: “We want to ask the President and his team to return that building back because we are ready to build a permanent memorial hall. Where younger generations, as they are growing up, see all the works that our great-grandpapa did for this country.” George urged participants to support the family’s appeal to the President, describing Macaulay as a courageous nationalist who regarded public office as service to the people rather than an avenue for personal gain. The post HERBERT MACAULAY@162: Nigeria’s devt doomed until we end primitive leadership selection — Jonathan appeared first on Vanguard News .
